title: Alive, or not quite?
question: Is a virus a living thing?
hook: It carries genes, reproduces and evolves, yet many biologists hesitate to call it alive.
idea: Viruses have some qualities of life but lack key ones, such as cell structure, so they have been called organisms at the edge of life.

beats.prompt: A single virus gets into a living cell. What often happens to that cell?

choices.label: It stays unchanged while the virus rests inside it
choices.feedback: A virus inside a cell is not resting; the cell is usually forced to make copies of it.

choices.label: It is forced to rapidly make thousands of copies of the virus
It destroys the virus and keeps the remains
choices.feedback: Cells do not usually win this way; the host cell is often forced to produce thousands of copies.

beats.explain: When infected, a host cell is often forced to rapidly produce thousands of copies of the original virus.

beats.prompt: Match each part of a virion to what it is.
pairs: Long molecules of DNA or RNA
A protein coat around the genes
An outside layer of lipids, present in some
beats.explain: A virion has genetic material, a protective capsid, and in some cases an outer lipid envelope.

beats.prompt: Sort each virus by how it spreads.
beats.explain: Influenza, measles and chickenpox spread in the air; norovirus and rotavirus pass by hand-to-mouth contact or in food or water.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Viruses are the most numerous type of biological entity.
A virus replicates only inside living cells.
So a virus left alone in pond water will keep multiplying.
beats.explain: Because a virus replicates only inside living cells, it cannot multiply on its own in water, however numerous viruses are.
